title: What is economics?
summary: Economics studies how societies use scarce resources to meet unlimited wants. Scarcity forces choices, every choice has an opportunity cost, and the PPC shows the trade-offs.

keyterms.definition: The situation where resources are limited relative to the unlimited wants and needs of people, so not every want can be satisfied.
The decision about how to use scarce resources, forced on individuals, firms and governments because of scarcity.
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
A good with zero opportunity cost because it is not scarce, e.g. air or sunlight in most places.
A good that is scarce and so has an opportunity cost to produce or consume.
The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Man-made goods used to produce other goods and services, e.g. machinery, tools, buildings and infrastructure.
The willingness and ability to organise the other factors of production and take risks to run a business.
A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all resources fully and efficiently employed, given technology.
An increase in real output (real GDP) over time; shown on a PPC by an outward shift of the curve.
The study of individual markets and the behaviour of consumers, firms and workers within them.
The study of the economy as a whole: total output, unemployment, inflation and growth.
Statements that can be tested against evidence; they describe what is, was or will be.
Statements involving value judgements about what ought to be; they cannot be tested as true or false.
A model showing how income, spending and factor services flow between households, firms, government and the foreign sector.
Leakages (saving, taxes, imports) remove income from the circular flow; injections (investment, government spending, exports) add to it.

questions.prompt: What is the basic economic problem?
options: Governments spend more than they earn
Firms always try to maximise profit
Resources are limited but wants are unlimited
questions.explanation: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants is the basic economic problem, which forces choices.
Every economy faces scarcity because resources are finite relative to wants; rich countries face it too.

questions.prompt: Maya has one free evening. She can work for $40, see a film or study. She prefers working to studying, and studies. What is her opportunity cost?
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is only the single next best alternative given up, not the sum of all alternatives.

questions.text: The value of the next best alternative given up is the ___.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures the real cost of any choice in terms of what is sacrificed.

questions.prompt: Match each factor of production with an example.

pairs.right: A delivery van owned by a firm
Starting a café and bearing the risk

questions.explanation: Land is natural resources, labour is human effort, capital is man-made means of production, entrepreneurship organises and takes risks.

questions.prompt: Which is a free good in most places?
questions.explanation: A free good has no opportunity cost. Public education is free at the point of use but uses scarce resources, so it is an economic good.

questions.statement: A government-provided school that charges no fees is a free good.
questions.explanation: It is still an economic good: teachers and buildings have an opportunity cost, paid for through taxes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is classed as capital in economics?
questions.explanation: In economics capital means physical man-made inputs; money and shares are financial assets, and oil underground is land.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning that links scarcity to opportunity cost.
items: Wants exceed what resources can produce
questions.explanation: Scarcity forces choice, and every choice has an opportunity cost: the next best alternative forgone.

questions.text: The study of individual markets, consumers and firms is called ___.
questions.explanation: Microeconomics looks at individual decision makers and markets; macroeconomics looks at the whole economy.

lessons.title: The PPC and the circular flow

questions.prompt: A point inside an economy’s PPC shows…
questions.explanation: Inside the PPC the economy could produce more of both goods; resources are unemployed or misallocated.

questions.prompt: Which event shifts a country’s PPC outward?
options: A rise in the price of exports
A move from producing cars to food
questions.explanation: Better technology raises productive capacity. Lower unemployment moves the economy towards the existing PPC, not shifting it.

questions.statement: A PPC that is bowed outward (concave) shows increasing opportunity cost.
questions.explanation: Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so producing more of one requires giving up ever larger amounts of the other.

questions.text: A straight-line PPC shows ___ opportunity cost.
questions.explanation: If resources are equally good at producing both goods, each extra unit costs the same amount of the other good.

questions.prompt: An economy moves along its PPC from point A (50 food, 20 machines) to point B (40 food, 30 machines). What is the opportunity cost of the extra 10 machines?
options: Zero, since the economy stays on the PPC
questions.explanation: Moving along the PPC, 10 food units are given up to gain 10 machines.

questions.prompt: Match each flow with its category in the circular flow model.
questions.explanation: Saving, taxes and imports are leakages; investment, government spending and exports are injections. Factor incomes flow to households in return for factor services.

questions.statement: If injections are greater than leakages, the size of the circular flow (national income) will tend to rise.
questions.explanation: More is entering the flow than leaving it, so income and output expand until a new equilibrium is reached.

questions.prompt: Which is an injection into the circular flow?
questions.explanation: Exports bring foreign spending into the domestic economy; the other three are leakages.

questions.prompt: Order these stages in the simple two-sector circular flow, starting with households.
items: Households supply factors of production to firms
Firms pay households wages, rent, interest and profit
Households spend their income on goods and services
Firms receive revenue and produce more output
questions.explanation: Real flows (factors, goods) go one way and money flows (incomes, spending) the other, so income = expenditure = output.

questions.text: Real output growth is shown on a PPC by an ___ shift of the curve.
questions.explanation: Economic growth raises the maximum possible output, shifting the PPC outward.
